# Introduction to Ezekiel

## Part 1: General Introduction

### Outline of Ezekiel

1. Yahweh calls Ezekiel to speak his words (1:1–3:27)
2. Yahweh judges Judah and Jerusalem (4:1–24:27)
3. Ezekiel prophesies against nearby nations (25:1–32:32)
4. Yahweh explains the fall of Jerusalem (33:1–33)
5. Ezekiel brings messages of hope (34:1–48:35)
  A. A new shepherd (34:1–31)
  B. Edom destroyed (35:1–15)
  C. Israel restored (36:1–37:28)
  D. Gog and Magog (38:1–39:29)
  E. Jerusalem and the temple restored (40:1–48:35)

### What is Ezekiel about?

The book of Ezekiel contains messages that Ezekiel prophesied between 593 B.C. and 571 B.C. The Jewish people, including Ezekiel, were exiled in Babylonia. Ezekiel told them that God was punishing them because they had sinned against him. He also said that God was going to further punish them by destroying Jerusalem and his temple. This happened in 586 B.C. After that, God gave Ezekiel messages that assured the people that God would restore them to their land. He said that God was using Babylon to punish them, but that eventually another nation would defeat the Babylonians. Ezekiel also prophesied about how God would restore Jerusalem and the temple so that the people could worship and sacrifice to him again. Ezekiel then described how the land would be divided again among the tribes of Israel.

### How should the title of this book be translated?

“Ezekiel” or “The Book of Ezekiel” is the traditional name for this book. Translators may also call it “The Messages from God Brought by Ezekiel.”

### Who wrote the book of Ezekiel?

Ezekiel wrote the prophecies in the book of Ezekiel. He was a prophet and priest who lived near Babylon in the time of the exile.

## Part 2: Important Religious and Cultural Concepts

### What was Ezekiel’s temple?

Several chapters of the book of Ezekiel give a detailed description of a new temple that Ezekiel sees in a vision. However, the temple that the people built after going back to Jerusalem was much smaller. Because Ezekiel’s temple has never been built, some scholars think that this temple is to be built in the future. Others think that it is a description of the heavenly, ideal temple. Other scholars think that Ezekiel’s temple is symbolic of the Church.

### Do the sacrifices in Ezekiel follow the law of Moses?

The sacrifices in Ezekiel 46 are somewhat different than the required sacrifices in Numbers 28. This may be because Ezekiel prophesied about a new temple with new sacrifices.

## Part 3: Important Translation Issues

### How should one represent Ezekiel’s visions in translation?

The book of Ezekiel has many complicated visions. These were things that God showed to Ezekiel, and many of them were visions of supernatural beings that are beyond human experience. Translators should avoid trying to explain these visions in their translations. Instead, they should present the visions just as they are in the source text. In some of the visions, God transported Ezekiel to other places. It seems clear that God allowed Ezekiel to see these places without physically going there.

### What does “know that I am Yahweh” mean?

This is a common phrase in the book of Ezekiel. Yahweh makes this statement after announcing either a severe punishment for people’s sin or a miraculous event in which he saves and restores his people. The phrase means that, after experiencing one of these things, the people will know who Yahweh is in the sense that he has all power and is in complete control of history. Since Yahweh announces the disaster or rescue ahead of when it happens, this also means that the people will know that Yahweh always does what he promises to do. Translate this phrase consistently throughout the book.

### “son of man”

The phrase “son of man” translates simply to “mortal man” or “human being,” reminding Ezekiel that despite receiving extraordinary divine visions, he remains a creature dependent on God. By repeatedly calling Ezekiel this throughout this book, Yahweh establishes a clear boundary between his infinite glory and the messenger’s earthly limitations.

### “spirit,” “breath,” or “wind”

The same Hebrew word can mean either “spirit,” “breath,” or “wind.” In biblical times, the concept of a person’s spirit was closely related to the concept of a person’s breath. The term can also refer to wind, that is, the movement of air in the natural world. Often there will be a note recommending how to translate this in specific contexts and the translation team will need to decide how to translate it in each case.

Ezekiel prophesied in Babylonia. When he mentions living “among the exiles,” he means he was one of the Israelite people whom the Babylonians had forcibly removed from the land of Judah. He begins the book describing visions he saw five years after the exile of King Jehoiachin.

# Ezekiel 2 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

1. Yahweh calls Ezekiel to speak to rebellious Israel (1–5)
2. Yahweh strengthens Ezekiel against their opposition (6–8)
3. Yahweh gives Ezekiel his words to proclaim (9–10)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### A house of rebellion

Yahweh repeatedly calls Israel “a house of rebellion,” picturing the people as a household marked by refusal to obey him.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

# Ezekiel 3 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter completes the commissioning of Ezekiel that began in chapter 2, and it ends with the prophet confined to his house and unable to speak unless Yahweh gives him a message.

1. Yahweh commissions Ezekiel as a watchman (1–11)
2. Yahweh’s Spirit strengthens and guides Ezekiel (12–15)
3. Yahweh holds Ezekiel responsible for warning the wicked (16–21)
4. Yahweh reveals his glory and commands Ezekiel to speak (22–27)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Eating the scroll

Yahweh commands Ezekiel to eat a scroll, and it tastes as sweet as honey. This symbolic act represents the prophet taking Yahweh’s message into himself, so that the words he speaks are Yahweh’s words and not his own.

### The prophet as a watchman

A watchman guarded an ancient city by looking out for danger and warning the people. In the same way, Ezekiel must warn the people of Yahweh’s judgment, and Yahweh holds him accountable for the death of anyone whom he fails to warn.

# Ezekiel 4 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Yahweh commands Ezekiel to perform a series of symbolic actions that portray the coming siege of Jerusalem and the famine that will accompany it.

1. Yahweh commands Ezekiel to portray Jerusalem’s siege (1–3)
2. Ezekiel bears Israel’s guilt and judgment (4–8)
3. Ezekiel portrays the famine and suffering of Jerusalem (9–17)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Symbolic actions

Ezekiel does not merely announce the siege of Jerusalem; he acts it out with a brick, an iron griddle, and his own body. Such enacted signs were a recognized form of prophecy and were understood to portray what Yahweh was about to do.

### Bearing iniquity

When Ezekiel “carries the iniquity” of Israel and of Judah, he is not being punished for his own sin. He is publicly representing the guilt of the people and the punishment that it deserves.

### Unclean food

The law of Moses forbade certain foods and required that food be prepared in ways that kept a person ritually pure. Baking bread over human excrement would defile both the food and the prophet, which is why Ezekiel protests in [4:14](../04/14.md).

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

Yahweh gives most of his instructions in this chapter with a Hebrew verb form that the ULT renders as “you shall.” These are instructions rather than predictions. Translate this form with the most natural way in your language for giving instructions.

### Weights and measures

The chapter states Ezekiel’s daily ration in shekels and in a fraction of a hin. You could keep these ancient units and explain them in a note, or you could give modern equivalents, as the UST does.

# Ezekiel 5 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter completes the series of symbolic actions that began in chapter 4 and then interprets them.

1. Yahweh judges Jerusalem for its rebellion (1–4)
2. Yahweh declares judgment because of Jerusalem’s abominations (5–10)
3. Yahweh brings famine, death, and scattering upon Jerusalem (11–17)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Symbolic actions

Ezekiel acts out the coming judgment rather than only announcing it. Shaving the head and beard was in itself a sign of mourning and humiliation, and each portion of the hair stands for a group of the people, as Yahweh explains in [5:12](../05/12.md).

### Defiling the sanctuary

Yahweh gives as a reason for this judgment that the people have brought detestable things into his temple. To make the sanctuary unclean was to treat as common the one place that Yahweh had set apart for himself.

### The curses of the covenant

Famine, the sword, plague, wild animals, and parents eating their own children are the very punishments that Yahweh had warned of in the law of Moses if his people broke the covenant. The first hearers would have recognized these disasters as covenant curses rather than as random calamities.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Shifting addressees

Yahweh addresses Ezekiel in verses 1–4 with a singular “you.” From verse 7 on, he addresses the city of Jerusalem and its people, and the “you” is sometimes singular and sometimes plural, occasionally within a single verse. You may need to make the addressee explicit, as the UST does.

### Quotations within quotations

The whole chapter is speech that Yahweh makes to Ezekiel, and within it he repeatedly introduces further quoted speech with “Thus says the Lord Yahweh.” If these nested quotations would be confusing, you could translate the inner quotations as indirect speech.

### Expressions for anger

The ULT preserves the Hebrew words for anger literally, speaking of Yahweh’s “nose” and his “heat” in [5:13](../05/13.md) and [5:15](../05/15.md). Many languages will need ordinary words for anger and wrath here, as the UST has.

# Ezekiel 6 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

In this chapter Yahweh tells Ezekiel to prophesy against the mountains of Israel, where the people worshiped idols.

1. Judgment on the places of idol worship (1–7)
    1. Yahweh commands Ezekiel to speak to the mountains of Israel (1–3)
    2. Yahweh will destroy the altars and leave the dead lying in front of the idols (4–7)
2. Some people will survive and remember Yahweh in exile (8–10)
3. Ezekiel is to lament over Israel’s coming destruction (11–14)
    1. The people will die by sword, famine, and plague (11–12)
    2. The dead will lie among the idols, and the land will become desolate (13–14)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### High places

The high places were hilltop sites where the Israelites built altars and set up idols to worship. Yahweh addresses the mountains, hills, stream beds, and valleys because that is where this idol worship took place, and he will defile those sites with the bodies of the people who worshiped there.

### Idolatry as prostitution

In [6:9](../06/09.md) Yahweh speaks of the people’s idol worship as if it were prostitution, that is, sexual unfaithfulness to him. This comparison appears often in Ezekiel.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Quotations within quotations

Yahweh speaks to Ezekiel, telling him to speak to the mountains, and in that speech Ezekiel quotes Yahweh, who again tells Ezekiel what to say, so the chapter has up to four levels of quotation. See [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-quotesinquotes]] for ways to make this clear.

### The identity of “you”

In verses 2 and 3, Yahweh tells Ezekiel to address his prophecy to the mountains of Israel. In verse 3, he begins speaking to the mountains using a plural “you” and “your.” The real audience for the prophecy is, of course, the people of Israel, and by verse 8 “you” has to refer to the people, so the two “audiences” have become blended. To make this clearer, you may wish to have “you” refer to the people throughout the chapter, as in the UST.

### “You will know that I am Yahweh”

This statement recurs throughout the chapter and the book. It means that when Yahweh carries out his judgment, the people will recognize that he is the true God who has all power and who does what he says. Translate it the same way each time it occurs.

Alternate translation: [And Yahweh spoke a message to me, saying]

# Ezekiel 7 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is a prophecy in poetic language announcing that the end has come for the land of Israel.

1. Yahweh tells Ezekiel to announce the end of the land of Israel (1–4)
2. The day of judgment is coming (5–13)
    1. The end has come because of the people’s ways (5–9)
    2. The day has arrived, and buying and selling will no longer matter (10–13)
3. The people will be helpless and will mourn (14–18)
4. Their wealth will not save them, and foreigners will defile Yahweh’s temple (19–22)
5. Yahweh will bring the nations, and no leader will be able to help (23–27)

Some translations set lines of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in [7:2–27](../07/02.md).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The day of Yahweh

Throughout this chapter, “the end,” “the time,” and “the day” refer to the time when Yahweh will punish the people of Israel for their sins.

### Mourning practices

In this culture, people expressed grief by wearing sackcloth and shaving their heads (v. 18). Ezekiel uses these practices to show how the people will mourn when Yahweh judges them.

### Ritual uncleanness

In verses 19–20, Yahweh compares the people’s silver and gold to the impurity of menstruation. Under the law of Moses, menstruation made a person ritually unclean as well as physically unclean, so the comparison shows that the people will regard their wealth as something that kept them from God and therefore as something detestable to be thrown away.

# Ezekiel 8 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter begins a vision that continues through chapter 11. Yahweh takes Ezekiel to the temple in Jerusalem and shows him a series of increasingly serious abominations that the people are committing there.

1. Ezekiel is carried in a vision from his house to Jerusalem (1–4)
2. Yahweh shows Ezekiel abominations in the temple (5–16)
    1. The image of jealousy north of the altar gate (5–6)
    2. Seventy elders burning incense to carved images (7–13)
    3. Women weeping for Tammuz (14–15)
    4. Twenty-five men worshiping the sun (16)
3. Yahweh says that he will punish them without pity (17–18)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Ezekiel’s vision of Jerusalem

Ezekiel was living among the exiles in Babylonia. He did not travel to Jerusalem physically; he saw the temple and what was happening there in a vision from God (v. 3).

### Idolatry in the temple

The temple was the place where the people were to worship only Yahweh, but the people of Judah were worshiping images of false gods there. For example, the “image of jealousy” was an idol that provoked Yahweh to be jealous (v. 3). Tammuz was a god of the Babylonians and other peoples, for whom women performed ritual weeping (v. 14). The men in verse 16 turned their backs on the temple to bow down to the sun.

# Ezekiel 9 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the vision that began in [Ezekiel 8](../08/01.md). Yahweh responds to the abominations that he showed Ezekiel in the temple by sending agents to punish Jerusalem.

1. Yahweh summons six executioners and a man clothed in linen (1–2)
2. Yahweh commands the man to mark the faithful and the others to kill everyone else (3–7)
3. Ezekiel pleads for the remnant, and Yahweh answers that he will not spare them (8–10)
4. The man clothed in linen reports that he has done what Yahweh commanded (11)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The glory of God leaving the cherub

In [9:3](../09/03.md), the glory of God moves from above the cherubs to the threshold of the temple. These cherubs would be the ones on the top of the ark of the covenant in the innermost sanctuary (Holy of Holies) in the temple. This is the first stage of a movement that continues in chapters 10 and 11, where God’s glory leaves the temple and then the city.

### The mark on the foreheads

The man clothed in linen puts a mark on the people who grieve over the abomination in the city, and the executioners must not harm anyone who has this mark. The mark identifies these people so that they will be protected, because they are true worshipers of Yahweh. The text does not say what the mark looked like, so a general word for “mark” is best.

### Judgment beginning at the sanctuary

Yahweh tells the executioners to begin at his sanctuary and to fill its courts with dead bodies. Dead bodies made a place ritually unclean, so this command shows that, because of the people’s sin, Yahweh was no longer treating the temple as holy.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Ezekiel’s report of a vision

Everything in this chapter is part of the vision that Ezekiel describes. God is showing these things to Ezekiel in Jerusalem without Ezekiel physically being in Jerusalem. # Ezekiel 10 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the vision that began in [Ezekiel 8](../08/01.md). The man clothed in linen carries out Yahweh’s command to scatter burning coals over Jerusalem, and the glory of Yahweh moves farther away from the temple.

1. Yahweh commands the man clothed in linen to take burning coals from among the cherubs (1–8)
    1. Yahweh gives the command (1–2)
    2. The cloud and the glory of Yahweh fill the temple and its courtyard (3–5)
    3. A cherub gives fire to the man (6–8)
2. Ezekiel describes the cherubs and their wheels (9–17)
3. The glory of Yahweh leaves the threshold and stops at the east gate (18–19)
4. Ezekiel recognizes these cherubs as the beings that he saw by the river of Kebar (20–22)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The glory of Yahweh leaving the temple

The glory of Yahweh moved to the threshold of the temple in [9:3](../09/03.md). In this chapter it moves again to the threshold (v. 4), then rests over the cherubs at the east gate (vv. 18–19). It leaves the city completely in [11:23](../11/23.md). This shows that Yahweh was abandoning the temple because of the people’s sin.

### The cherubs and the wheels

The beings and wheels in this chapter are the same ones that Ezekiel saw in chapter 1, where he called them “beings.” Here he says that he realized they were cherubs (v. 20). Translators may want to use the same words for the faces, wings, wheels, and eyes as in chapter 1.

The ULT puts verses 3, 8, and 20–22 in parentheses because they give background information that interrupts the main events. Use whatever way your language has of marking background information.

# Ezekiel 11 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter concludes the vision that began in [Ezekiel 8:1](../08/01.md), in which the Spirit carries Ezekiel to Jerusalem and shows him the sins of its people and Yahweh’s judgment on them.

1. Yahweh condemns the leaders of Jerusalem (1–13)
    1. Ezekiel sees 25 men at the east gate of the temple (1–4)
    2. Ezekiel prophesies against them (5–12)
    3. Pelatiah dies, and Ezekiel cries out to Yahweh (13)
2. Yahweh promises to restore the exiles (14–21)
3. The glory of Yahweh leaves the city, and Ezekiel returns to the exiles (22–25)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The departure of Yahweh’s glory

In [11:22–23](../11/22.md), the [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/glory]] of Yahweh rises with the [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/cherubim]] and leaves Jerusalem, stopping on the mountain east of the city. This completes the departure that began in chapters 9 and 10 and shows that Yahweh has abandoned the city to judgment.

### Yahweh’s presence with the exiles

The people who remained in Jerusalem claimed that the land belonged to them because the [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/exile]]s were far from Yahweh. Yahweh answers that he himself has been a [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/sanctuary]] for the exiles and that he will bring them back and give them a new heart and a new spirit so that they will obey him.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### The image of the pot and the meat

In [11:3](../11/03.md), the leaders of Jerusalem compare the city to a cooking pot and themselves to the meat in it, meaning that the city would protect them. Yahweh takes up the same image in [11:7](../11/07.md) and [11:11](../11/11.md) and turns it against them. Translate the image consistently in all three verses so that readers can see how Yahweh reverses it.

### Pronouns for the city

The ULT refers to Jerusalem as “she” and “her” throughout this chapter because the Hebrew word for “city” is feminine. If this would confuse readers in your language, you could use “it” or “the city.”

# Ezekiel 20 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Yahweh refuses to let the elders of Israel inquire of him and instead has Ezekiel recount Israel’s long history of rebellion, followed by a promise of judgment and restoration.

1. The elders come to inquire of Yahweh, and he refuses them (1–4)
2. Yahweh recounts Israel’s rebellion against him (5–29)
    1. In Egypt (5–9)
    2. The first generation in the wilderness (10–17)
    3. The second generation in the wilderness (18–26)
    4. In the land Yahweh gave them (27–29)
3. Yahweh condemns the idolatry of the present generation (30–32)
4. Yahweh promises to judge his people and bring them back to their land (33–44)
5. Yahweh’s message against the forest of the south (45–49)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Acting for the sake of his name

Yahweh repeatedly holds back his punishment so that his name, meaning his reputation, would not be profaned among the nations who had seen him rescue Israel from Egypt. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/profane]])

### Sabbaths and idols

The chapter presents keeping Yahweh’s Sabbaths as a sign of his relationship with Israel, and worshiping idols at the high places as breaking that relationship. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/sabbath]], [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/falsegod]], and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/highplaces]]) Verses 26 and 31 refer to the practice of sacrificing children to idols.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Repeated refrain

Each stage of the history in verses 5–22 follows the same pattern: Yahweh gives a command, the people rebel, Yahweh decides to pour out his anger, and then he holds back for the sake of his name. Translating these repeated expressions consistently will help readers see the pattern.

### Verse numbering

In the Hebrew text, verses 45–49 are numbered as 21:1–5. Translations may follow either numbering system.

If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [harmful laws by which they could not truly live]

The implication is that Yahweh allowed the Israelites to follow harmful practices as a punishment for rejecting his good statutes. Some interpreters think Yahweh means that he let them follow the laws and customs of the nations. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [statutes that were not good for them, as a punishment]

Yahweh is referring to sacrificing children by burning them alive in a polite way, using the phrase **making every firstborn of the womb to pass**. Depending on what is helpful for your readers, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [in making every firstborn of the womb to pass through the fire as a sacrifice]

Ezekiel is using this possessive form to mean the firstborn children who open the womb, that is, the first child born to each mother. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [every firstborn child]

The first **so that** marks “I might desolate them” as the goal or purpose of “I made them unclean by their gifts”. The second **so that** marks what follows as the goal or purpose of Yahweh making them desolate. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.
The term translated as **Therefore** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [Because of all this]

Quote: דַּבֵּ֨ר אֶל־בֵּ֤ית יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ & וְ⁠אָמַרְתָּ֣ אֲלֵי⁠הֶ֔ם כֹּ֥ה אָמַ֖ר אֲדֹנָ֣⁠י יְהוִ֑ה
Note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [tell the house of Israel…that this is what the Lord Yahweh says to them]

The pronoun **this** refers to the sinful acts that Yahweh describes in the next verse. Some interpreters think it refers back to the rebellions in the wilderness that Yahweh has just described. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Still by what I will now describe, your fathers blasphemed me]
If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **violation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [when they were very unfaithful to me]

Ezekiel is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [when they were utterly unfaithful to me]
See how you handled the similar expression in [20:6](../20/06.md).

Quote: כָל גִּבְעָ֨ה רָמָ֜ה וְ⁠כָל עֵ֣ץ עָבֹ֗ת
Note: The implication is that the Israelites worshiped idols on **every high hill** and under **every leafy tree**, because people thought that those were good places to worship false gods. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [every high hill and every leafy tree, places where people worshiped false gods]

Ezekiel is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [and they offered their offerings there]

Here, **the anger of their offering** represents “their offering that made me angry.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [their offering that provoked me]
See how you translated the similar expression in [6:13](../06/13.md). This also occurs in verse 41.

Quote: וָ⁠אֹמַ֣ר אֲלֵ⁠הֶ֔ם מָ֣ה הַ⁠בָּמָ֔ה אֲשֶׁר־אַתֶּ֥ם הַ⁠בָּאִ֖ים שָׁ֑ם
Note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [And I asked them what the high place was to which they were going]

Quote: מָ֣ה הַ⁠בָּמָ֔ה אֲשֶׁר אַתֶּ֥ם הַ⁠בָּאִ֖ים שָׁ֑ם
Note: Yahweh is using the question form to rebuke the Israelites for worshiping at the high place. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You should not be going to this high place to worship!]

Quote: וַ⁠יִּקָּרֵ֤א שְׁמָ⁠הּ֙ בָּמָ֔ה עַ֖ד הַ⁠יּ֥וֹם הַ⁠זֶּֽה
Note: Yahweh is providing background information to help readers understand why that place was called **Bamah**. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

The expression **its name was called** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And people have called it Bamah]
The word **Bamah** is the name of a place. It is the same word that is translated as **the high place** earlier in this verse. You could include its meaning in your translation or in a footnote.

Quote: לָ⁠כֵ֞ן אֱמֹ֣ר אֶל־בֵּ֣ית יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל כֹּ֤ה אָמַר֙ אֲדֹנָ֣⁠י יְהוִ֔ה
Note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Therefore, tell the house of Israel that the Lord Yahweh says this]
The term translated as **Therefore** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [For this reason]

Quote: הַ⁠בְּ⁠דֶ֥רֶךְ אֲבֽוֹתֵי⁠כֶ֖ם אַתֶּ֣ם נִטְמְאִ֑ים וְ⁠אַחֲרֵ֥י שִׁקּוּצֵי⁠הֶ֖ם אַתֶּ֥ם זֹנִֽים
Note: Yahweh is using the question form to accuse the Israelites of doing the same evil things that their ancestors did. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You are making yourselves unclean in the way of your fathers, and you are prostituting yourselves after their detestations!]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the conduct of the ancestors of the Israelites were a **way**, that is, a path. It means that the Israelites were behaving in the same way as their ancestors. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [By acting just as your fathers did]
Here, **your fathers** represents “your ancestors.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [your forefathers]
If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **detestations**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the detestable things they did]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if worshiping idols were **prostituting yourselves**. It means that by worshiping other gods, the Israelites were being unfaithful to Yahweh, just as a prostitute is sexually unfaithful. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [are you behaving disloyally toward me]

Ezekiel is using **when you lifted your gifts** as a common expression of the culture to mean “when you offered your sacrifices to the gods.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And when you presented your gifts] or [And when you offered your sacrifices]
See how you handled the similar expression in [20:26](../20/26.md).

Yahweh is using the question form to emphasize that he will not let the Israelites seek him for guidance. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [And I will certainly not be sought by you, house of Israel!]

Here, **house of Israel** represents the people who are descendants of Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [people of Israel]

Quote: חַי אָ֗נִי נְאֻם֙ אֲדֹנָ֣⁠י יְהוִ֔ה אִם אִדָּרֵ֖שׁ לָ⁠כֶֽם
Note: Following the custom of the culture, Yahweh is swearing an oath by stating the first part of a condition (“if”) but not the second part (“then”). Yahweh means that he will certainly not let the Israelites seek him for guidance. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explicitly state the second part of this condition. Alternate translation: [As surely as I live”—the declaration of the Lord Yahweh—“I will certainly not let you seek me for guidance]

Yahweh is using **the thing ascending on your spirit** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the thoughts coming into your mind.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And the thing that comes into your mind]

Ezekiel is repeating forms of the verb **being** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [it will certainly not happen]

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [that you are saying that you want to become like the nations]

Here, **wood and stone** represent “idols made from wood and stone.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to serve idols made from wood and stone]

Quote: חַי אָ֕נִי נְאֻ֖ם אֲדֹנָ֣⁠י יְהוִ֑ה אִם לֹ֠א
Note: Following the custom of the culture, Yahweh is swearing an oath by stating the first part of a condition (“if”) but not the second part (“then”). By saying **if not**, Yahweh means that he will certainly do what he says next. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explicitly state the second part of this condition. Alternate translation: [As surely as I live”—the declaration of the Lord Yahweh—“it is certain that]

The terms **with a strong hand** and **with an outstretched arm** mean similar things. Both refer to the great power of Yahweh. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. This also occurs in verse 34. Alternate translation: [with very great power]

The expression **heat poured out** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. This also occurs in verse 34. Alternate translation: [and with heat that I pour out]

Yahweh is using the phrase **and with heat poured out** as a common expression of the culture to mean “and with a great expression of anger.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and with burning rage] or [and with intense anger]

The expression **you were scattered** is a passive verbal form. Yahweh is the one who scattered them. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [in which I scattered you]

Quote: בְּ⁠יָ֤ד חֲזָקָה֙ וּ⁠בִ⁠זְר֣וֹעַ נְטוּיָ֔ה וּ⁠בְ⁠חֵמָ֖ה שְׁפוּכָֽה
Note: See how you translated the similar expressions in [20:33](../20/33.md).

The implication is that **the wilderness of the peoples** is a desert region among the nations where Yahweh would judge the Israelites, just as he judged their ancestors in the wilderness after they left Egypt. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the desert region among the nations, a wilderness like the one where I judged your ancestors]

Yahweh is using **face to face** as a common expression of the culture to mean “directly and personally.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [directly and personally]

Here, Yahweh is speaking as if he were a shepherd and the Israelites were sheep that he would make **pass under the rod**. A shepherd would hold his rod over his sheep as they passed by in order to count and examine them. It means that Yahweh would carefully examine each of the Israelites. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I will carefully examine each one of you]

Here, Yahweh is speaking as if the covenant were a **bond** that tied the Israelites to him. It means that Yahweh would make the Israelites keep his covenant. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [under the obligation of the covenant]

Ezekiel is using the possessive form to describe a **bond** that is characterized by **the covenant**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [into the binding obligation of the covenant]

Here, Yahweh is speaking as if the rebels were impurities that he would **purge** from metal. It means that he would remove the rebels from among the Israelites. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And I will remove from among you the rebels]
If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **sojournings**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [From the land where they have been staying temporarily]

Ezekiel is using the possessive form to describe a land where the people have been living as foreigners. The expression **the land of their sojournings** means “the land in which they have lived as foreigners.” If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [From the land where they have lived as foreigners]

In this verse, the word **he** is singular in form, but it refers to all the rebels as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “he.” Alternate translation: [but to the land of Israel, they will not come]

Yahweh actually means to communicate the opposite of the literal meaning of what he is saying here. He does not want the Israelites to serve their idols. If a speaker of your language would not do that, you could translate the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Each man, go ahead and serve his idols, if you insist on doing that]

Here, the masculine term **A man** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [Any man or woman, their idols]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and afterward keep on serving them, if you are not going to listen to me]

Ezekiel is using **A man** as a common expression of the culture to mean “each person.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Each of you] or [Everybody]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a **name** that is characterized by **holiness**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [my holy name]

Here, **the name of my holiness** represents Yahweh himself, who is holy. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [me, Yahweh, who is holy]

The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because]

The implication is that **the mountain of my holiness** is Mount Zion in Jerusalem, where the temple was. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [on Mount Zion in Jerusalem, the mountain of my holiness where my temple is, on the mountain of the height of Israel]

Ezekiel is using this possessive form to mean the mountain that is set apart for Yahweh, which is holy because it belongs to him. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [on my holy mountain]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a **mountain** that is characterized by **height**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [on the high mountain of Israel]

Here, Yahweh is speaking as if the Israelites were a sacrifice with **an aroma of pleasing** that he would **accept**. It means that Yahweh would be pleased with the Israelites and accept them, just as he was pleased with sacrifices that people offered to him properly. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [With great pleasure, I will accept you]

Ezekiel is using the possessive form to describe an aroma that is characterized by being **pleasing**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [With a pleasing aroma]

The expression **I will be sanctified** is a passive verbal form. It means that the nations will see that Yahweh is holy. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [then I will show myself to be holy among you]

Here, **to the eyes of the nations** represents the nations seeing what Yahweh does. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in the sight of the nations]

Quote: אֶל־אַדְמַ֣ת יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל אֶל־הָ⁠אָ֗רֶץ אֲשֶׁ֤ר נָשָׂ֨אתִי֙ אֶת־יָדִ֔⁠י לָ⁠תֵ֥ת אוֹתָ֖⁠הּ לַ⁠אֲבֽוֹתֵי⁠כֶֽם
Note: The terms **to the land of Israel** and **to the land that I lifted my hand to give it to your fathers** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two phrases together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [to the land of Israel that I promised to give to your fathers]

Lifting the hand was a symbolic action by which Yahweh showed that he was solemnly swearing a promise. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [that I solemnly promised to give]
Here, **your fathers** represents “your ancestors.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to your forefathers]

By **there**, Ezekiel means in the land of Israel, where God will bring the people back. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [in that land of Israel]

Here Ezekiel is speaking of how a person lives as if that were a **way** or path that the person was walking along. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [how you lived]
Alternate translation: [with which you defiled yourselves]
See how you translated this expression in [6:9](../06/09.md).
If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **evils**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [by all the evil things that you did]
Ezekiel is using the term **name** to represent who the person is or to refer to the person’s reputation. Alternate translation: [my reputation]

The phrases **your evil ways** and **your ruined deeds** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two phrases together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [not according to all the very wicked things that you have done]

Here Ezekiel is speaking of how a person lives as if that were a **way** or path that the person was walking along. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [according to your evil behavior]

Yahweh is using **set your face** as a common expression of the culture to mean “to turn one’s attention towards something in order to oppose it.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [focus your attention toward Teman in order to oppose it]

The terms **the way** and **Teman** mean similar things. Ezekiel is using the two terms together to mean “the way toward Teman.” If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [toward Teman]
The words **Teman** and **Darom** are names for the region to the south. Both words mean “south,” so you could also translate them as “the south.”

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the words of Ezekiel were a liquid that he could **drivel**, that is, cause to drip. It means that Ezekiel should speak his prophecy against the south. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and speak your prophecy against Darom]

Ezekiel is speaking to **the forest of the field of the Negev**, which he knows cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about the coming judgment on the land. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about **the forest of the field of the Negev**. Alternate translation: [the people of the southern land]

The word **Negev** is a Hebrew word that refers to a southern desert region of the land of Israel. You will need to decide if you will use this word in its Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew word, you could spell it the way it sounds in your language and then put the translation in a footnote. Alternate translation: [the southern region]

Quote: וְ⁠אָֽמַרְתָּ֙ לְ⁠יַ֣עַר הַ⁠נֶּ֔גֶב שְׁמַ֖ע דְּבַר יְהוָ֑ה כֹּֽה אָמַ֣ר אֲדֹנָ֣⁠י יְהוִ֡ה
Note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [And you shall tell the forest of the Negev to hear the word of Yahweh, for this is what the Lord Yahweh says]

Yahweh is telling Ezekiel to speak to **the forest of the Negev**, which cannot hear him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if Ezekiel were speaking directly to the people of Judah. Alternate translation: [And you shall say to the people of Judah, whom the forest of the Negev represents]

Yahweh is using **Look at me** as a common expression of the culture to mean “I am about to.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am about to kindle]
The word **you** is singular here because Yahweh is addressing **the forest of the Negev**, so use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Here Yahweh is speaking as if his judgment were **a fire** that he would kindle in a forest. It means that he would destroy the people of Judah. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [bringing on you a judgment that is like a fire]

Yahweh is speaking of **a fire** as if it were a living thing that could **eat**. It means that the fire would burn up everything. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and it will burn up in you]

Quote: כָל עֵֽץ לַח֩ וְ⁠כָל עֵ֨ץ יָבֵ֤שׁ
Note: Yahweh is referring to all of the trees in the forest by naming two major components: **every fresh tree** and **every dry tree**. Since the forest represents the people of Judah, this means all the people of Judah. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [every tree without exception]

The expression **will not be quenched** is a passive verbal form. It means that no one will be able to put out the fire. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [No one will be able to extinguish the flame of the blaze]
Ezekiel is using this possessive form to mean a flame that comes from a blazing fire. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The flaming fire]

Quote: וְ⁠נִצְרְבוּ בָ֥⁠הּ כָּל פָּנִ֖ים מִ⁠נֶּ֥גֶב צָפֽוֹנָ⁠ה
Note: The expression **will be scorched by it** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and it will scorch all faces from the south to the north]

Yahweh is using **all faces** to represent every part of the forested land. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [all land]

Yahweh is referring to all of the land by naming two major components: **the south** and **the north**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in the whole land]

Yahweh is using **all flesh** to represent all people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And all people will see]

The pronoun **it** refers to the fire that Yahweh kindled. Some interpreters think it refers to the forest that the fire burned. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [I, Yahweh, have caused that fire to burn]

The expression **It will not be quenched** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is people. Alternate translation: [No one will put it out]
See how you translated this phrase in [4:14](../04/14.md).

Quote: הֵ֚מָּה אֹמְרִ֣ים לִ֔⁠י הֲ⁠לֹ֛א מְמַשֵּׁ֥ל מְשָׁלִ֖ים הֽוּא
Note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [They are saying about me that I am just a user of proverbs]

The people are using the question form to mock Ezekiel and to show that they did not take his message seriously. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [He is just a user of proverbs!]

The pronoun **he** refers to Ezekiel himself. The people are speaking about Ezekiel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Is this Ezekiel not a user of proverbs]

Here, **a user of proverbs** is an emphatic construction that uses a verb and its object that come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of showing the emphasis.

# Ezekiel 21 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is a series of oracles about the sword that Yahweh sends in judgment, first against Jerusalem and the land of Israel and then against the Ammonites.

1. Yahweh draws his sword against Jerusalem and the land of Israel (1–7)
    1. The sword comes out of its sheath (1–5)
    2. Ezekiel groans as a sign of the coming disaster (6–7)
2. The song of the sword (8–17)
3. The king of Babylon chooses the road to Jerusalem (18–27)
    1. The king uses divination at the fork in the road (18–23)
    2. Yahweh announces judgment on Jerusalem and its prince (24–27)
4. The sword against the Ammonites (28–32)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in [21:9–17](../21/09.md).

The ULT follows the verse numbering of most English translations. In the Hebrew text, verses 1–32 of this chapter are numbered 21:6–37, because the Hebrew chapter begins with the verses that the ULT numbers as 20:45–49.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The sword of Yahweh

The [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/sword]] in this chapter represents the army of [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/names/babylon]] that Yahweh sends to punish his people and the people of [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/names/ammon]]. Yahweh speaks of it as his own sword to show that he is the one bringing this judgment.

### Divination

In verses 21–22, the king of Babylon uses three kinds of [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/divination]] to decide which city to attack: shaking arrows, consulting household idols, and examining the liver of a sacrificed animal. Yahweh controls even these pagan practices so that the king goes to Jerusalem.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Symbolic actions

Ezekiel groans, strikes his hands together, and marks out two roads as signs to the people (verses 6, 14, and 19). See [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/translate-symaction]].

# Ezekiel 22 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter contains three messages from Yahweh that list the sins of Jerusalem and of all Israel and announce his judgment on them.

1. Yahweh accuses Jerusalem, the city of blood (1–16)
    1. Jerusalem’s bloodshed and idols make her guilty and unclean (1–5)
    2. Yahweh lists the sins committed in the city (6–12)
    3. Yahweh will scatter the people among the nations (13–16)
2. Yahweh will melt Israel like metal in a furnace (17–22)
3. All the leaders and people of the land are guilty (23–31)
    1. Prophets, priests, princes, and people have all sinned (23–29)
    2. No one stands in the gap, so Yahweh pours out his wrath (30–31)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The city of blood

Yahweh calls Jerusalem “the city of blood” because many people were murdered there and the leaders used violence to gain wealth. See [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/bloodshed]].

### Refining metal

In verses 18–22, Yahweh compares Israel to the worthless material left over when silver is melted in a [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/furnace]]. Just as a metalworker melts metal with fire, Yahweh will gather his people into Jerusalem and punish them there.

### Holy and common

The priests were supposed to teach the people the difference between what was [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/holy]] and what was common, and between what was clean and unclean. Instead, they profaned Yahweh’s holy things and ignored his Sabbaths, so that Yahweh himself was profaned among them (verse 26). See [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/profane]].

# Ezekiel 23 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is an extended allegory in which Yahweh describes Samaria and Jerusalem as two sisters who became his wives and then were unfaithful to him.

1. Two sisters, Oholah and Oholibah, prostitute themselves in Egypt and become Yahweh’s wives (1–4)
2. Oholah (Samaria) lusts after the Assyrians and is punished by them (5–10)
3. Oholibah (Jerusalem) becomes even more corrupt than her sister (11–21)
    1. She lusts after the Assyrians (11–13)
    2. She lusts after the Babylonians and then turns away from them (14–18)
    3. She returns to the prostitution of her youth in Egypt (19–21)
4. Yahweh announces his judgment on Oholibah (22–35)
    1. Her former lovers will attack and humiliate her (22–27)
    2. Yahweh will give her into the hands of those she hates (28–31)
    3. She will drink the cup of her sister (32–34)
    4. She will bear the consequences of forgetting Yahweh (35)
5. Yahweh accuses and judges both sisters (36–49)
    1. They committed adultery, sacrificed their children, and defiled Yahweh’s sanctuary (36–42)
    2. Righteous men will judge them as adulteresses and murderers (43–45)
    3. An assembly will stone them and destroy their houses (46–49)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Prostitution as unfaithfulness to Yahweh

Yahweh pictures his covenant with Israel as a marriage. When Samaria and Jerusalem worshiped idols and trusted in foreign nations such as Egypt, Assyria, and Babylon, it was like a wife committing [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/adultery]] or acting as a [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/prostitute]]. See [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/covenant]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/falsegod]].

### The cup of judgment

In verses 31–34, Yahweh speaks of the punishment he will give Jerusalem as a cup that she must drink. The cup is the same punishment that Samaria received, and drinking it will make Jerusalem like a drunken person who suffers horror and desolation.

### Child sacrifice

In verses 37–39, Yahweh accuses the two sisters of killing their children as sacrifices to idols and then coming into his [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/sanctuary]] on the same day, which profaned it. See [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/profane]].

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Oholah and Oholibah

The name “Oholah” means “her tent,” and “Oholibah” means “my tent is in her.” Verse 4 explains that Oholah represents Samaria and Oholibah represents Jerusalem. Consider whether to keep these names throughout the allegory or to explain their meaning in a footnote. See [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/translate-names]].

### Sexual language

This chapter uses very explicit sexual language to show how shameful the sins of Samaria and Jerusalem were. If such language would be offensive in your culture, consider using polite expressions that still communicate the seriousness of the sins. See [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-euphemism]].

### Shifts in person

Yahweh speaks about the sisters as “she” and “they” in much of the chapter, but he also addresses Oholibah as “you” beginning in verse 21 and shifts between “you” and “her” in verses 40–44. Consider how to make these shifts clear in your language. See [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-123person]].

# Ezekiel 24 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter contains Ezekiel’s last messages of judgment against Jerusalem before the city falls, dated to the day the Babylonian army began its siege of the city.

1. Yahweh tells Ezekiel to record the date the siege of Jerusalem began (1–2)
2. The parable of the cooking pot (3–14)
    1. The pot is filled with choice meat and boiled (3–5)
    2. Woe to the city of bloodshed, which is like a rusted pot (6–8)
    3. Yahweh will heat the empty pot until its rust burns away (9–12)
    4. Yahweh will not relent in punishing Jerusalem (13–14)
3. The death of Ezekiel’s wife is a sign to the people (15–24)
    1. Yahweh forbids Ezekiel to mourn for his wife (15–18)
    2. Ezekiel explains what his actions mean for the people (19–24)
4. Ezekiel will no longer be mute when a survivor brings news from Jerusalem (25–27)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in [24:3–12](../24/03.md).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Uncovered blood

The law of Moses required people to cover with dust the blood of animals they killed, and blood left uncovered on a bare rock was thought to call out for vengeance. In [24:7–8](../24/07.md), Jerusalem has shed blood openly, so Yahweh leaves that blood exposed as a witness against the city.

### Mourning customs

In this culture, people mourned by removing their turbans and sandals, covering the lower part of their faces, and eating food that neighbors brought to them. Yahweh forbids Ezekiel to do any of these things to show that the people will be too overwhelmed by the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple to mourn properly. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/mourn]])

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### The cooking pot metaphor

In [24:3–12](../24/03.md), the pot represents Jerusalem, the meat represents its people, and the rust represents the city’s persistent guilt. The text moves back and forth between speaking about the pot (“it”) and the city (“her”), so make sure your translation shows that both refer to Jerusalem. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/parable]])

### Ezekiel as a sign

Ezekiel’s actions in this chapter are a sign that shows the people what will happen to them, and in [24:24](../24/24.md) Yahweh refers to Ezekiel by name. In [24:27](../24/27.md), Yahweh says that the muteness that began in [3:26](../03/26.md) will end when the news of Jerusalem’s fall arrives. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/sign]])

# Ezekiel 25 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter begins a series of prophecies against the nations around Israel that continues through chapter 32. It contains four short judgment speeches, each against a neighbor that treated Judah’s fall with scorn.

1. Judgment on Ammon (1–7)
    1. Ammon said “Aha!” over the temple, the land, and the exiles (1–5)
    2. Ammon rejoiced with contempt over the land of Israel (6–7)
2. Judgment on Moab (8–11)
3. Judgment on Edom (12–14)
4. Judgment on Philistia (15–17)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Yahweh’s judgment on nations that scorned Judah

Ammon, Moab, Edom, and the Philistines each mocked Judah or took revenge on it when Babylon destroyed the temple and sent the people into exile. Yahweh treats this as an offense against himself and his people, and he declares that he will punish them.

### “You will know that I am Yahweh”

Most of these prophecies end by saying that the punished nation will know that “I am Yahweh.” This shows that the purpose of the judgment is for these nations to recognize Yahweh’s power and authority.

# Ezekiel 26 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter begins a series of prophecies against the city of Tyre that continues through [28:19](../28/19.md). It contains four messages from Yahweh, each beginning with “thus says the Lord Yahweh.”

1. Yahweh will judge Tyre because it rejoiced over the fall of Jerusalem (1–6)
2. Nebuchadnezzar will besiege and destroy Tyre (7–14)
3. The rulers of the coastlands will mourn over Tyre (15–18)
    1. The princes of the sea mourn (15–16)
    2. The princes sing a lament over Tyre (17–18)
4. Yahweh will bring Tyre down to the pit (19–21)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in [26:17–18](../26/17.md).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Tyre

Tyre was a wealthy Phoenician trading city built on a rocky island just off the coast, with towns that depended on it on the mainland. Other peoples who traded by sea relied on it, so its fall would shock all of the coastlands.

### Mourning for a fallen city

The princes of the sea take off their fine robes, sit on the ground, and sing a funeral song over Tyre. These were common ways to show great grief. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/mourn]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/lament]])

### The pit

In verses 19–21, Yahweh speaks of Tyre going down to “the pit” and “the land of the lower parts.” These expressions refer to the place of the dead and indicate that Tyre will be destroyed completely and never exist again. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/pit]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/hades]])

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Changes in how Tyre is referred to

Yahweh speaks to Tyre as “you” but also describes the city as “she” and “her,” sometimes moving from one to the other within a few verses (for example, in verses 3–6 and 17). In the same way, the attackers are called “they” in some verses and “he” (Nebuchadnezzar) in others. Consider whether your language needs to use the same form throughout.

### Quotations within quotations

Yahweh tells Ezekiel what to say, Ezekiel’s message quotes Yahweh, and Yahweh quotes both what Tyre said and what the princes will say. Consider whether your language needs to show these levels of quotation in a simpler way.

# Ezekiel 27 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is a funeral song (lament) over the city of Tyre. It continues the prophecies against Tyre that began in chapter 26. Most of the song describes Tyre as a magnificent trading ship that sinks in the middle of the sea.

  1. Yahweh tells Ezekiel to sing a lament over Tyre (1–3)
  2. Tyre is pictured as a beautiful ship (4–11)
    1. The ship is built from the finest materials (4–7)
    2. Men from other cities serve as its crew and soldiers (8–11)
  3. The many nations that traded with Tyre (12–25)
  4. The ship is wrecked in the heart of the seas (26–27)
  5. The sailors and the coastlands mourn over Tyre (28–36)
    1. The sailors weep and mourn (28–31)
    2. The sailors sing their own lament over Tyre (32–36)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in [27:3–11](../27/03.md) and [27:25–36](../27/25.md). Verses 12–25 are a list of trading partners written as prose.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Tyre’s sea trade

Tyre was a wealthy Phoenician port whose ships carried goods among many peoples. Verses 12–25 name those peoples and the goods they traded, showing how far Tyre’s trade reached and how rich it had become. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/names/tyre]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/names/tarshish]])

### Mourning customs

In verses 30–31 the sailors throw dust on their heads, roll in ashes, shave their heads, and put on sackcloth. These were common ways to show great grief. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/mourn]], [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/lament]], and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/sackcloth]])

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Tyre as a ship

In verses 4–11 and 25–36, Yahweh speaks of the city of Tyre as if it were a ship, describing its planks, mast, sails, rowers, and cargo. The wreck of the ship represents the destruction of the city. If possible, keep this extended metaphor in your translation, since it runs through most of the chapter.

### Place names and trade goods

The chapter lists many places, peoples, and goods that may be unknown in your culture, and the meaning of some of the Hebrew words is uncertain. You may want to use general terms for goods that your readers would not recognize. Additionally the phrasing for trading or buying frequently uses ‘gave,’ you may want to use a more natural term for buying and selling.

### Past tense for future events

Although the sinking of Tyre had not yet happened, verses 26 and 34 describe it as if it were already past. This shows that it will certainly happen. Consider whether your language would express this with a future form.

### They, they
Especially in verses 10-24 pronouns which appear on the verb are also expressed independently. This may have one or more of the follow effects which you may wish to implement in a natural way in your language: 1) marking a new subject (nation) as the topic, 2) creating a list structure, 3) signaling that Tyre’s perfect beauty was actually from all the other nations that traded with her.

# Ezekiel 28 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter concludes the prophecies against Tyre that began in chapter 26. It then gives a short prophecy against Sidon, the neighboring Phoenician city, and ends with a promise that Yahweh will restore Israel to its land.

1. Yahweh condemns the ruler of Tyre for claiming to be a god (1–10)
    1. The ruler’s wisdom and wealth made him proud (1–5)
    2. Foreigners will kill him and bring him down to the pit (6–10)
2. A lament over the king of Tyre (11–19)
    1. The king is pictured as a cherub in Eden, the garden of God (11–15)
    2. Yahweh throws the king down and destroys him (16–19)
3. Yahweh will judge Sidon (20–24)
4. Yahweh will gather Israel and let them live safely in their land (25–26)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter


### Eden and the cherub

In verses 12–16, the lament describes the king of Tyre as if he had been in [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/names/eden]], covered with precious stones, and as if he had been a guardian [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/cherubs]] on the holy mountain of God until he sinned and was thrown out. In addition to being about the king of Tyre, Christians have often viewed this as speaking about the fall of Satan (or Adam), translators should attempt to translate the text as it is and leave the interpretation to others.

### Dying uncircumcised

Dying while uncircumcised implied being an enemy of Yahweh and thus one would go down to “the pit,” which was the place of the dead, perhaps the “bad” part of the place of the dead. This shows that the ruler of Tyre would die like an other enemy of Yahweh. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/circumcise]] and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/pit]])

# Ezekiel 29 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter begins a series of prophecies against Egypt that continues through chapter 32. It contains two dated messages from Yahweh. The second, given about 16 years after the first, is the latest dated prophecy in the book.

  1. Yahweh will judge Pharaoh and Egypt (1–16)
    1. Pharaoh, the sea monster, will be pulled out of his rivers and left to die (1–5)
    2. Egypt failed Israel like a staff made of reed (6–7)
    3. Egypt will be desolate and its people scattered for 40 years (8–12)
    4. Yahweh will bring the Egyptians back, but only as a lowly kingdom (13–16)
  2. Yahweh gives Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar (17–21)
    1. Nebuchadnezzar received no wages for his campaign against Tyre (17–18)
    2. Egypt will be his army’s wages (19–20)
    3. Yahweh will make a horn sprout for Israel (21)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Pharaoh as a sea monster

Yahweh pictures [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/names/pharaoh]] as a great creature lying in the Nile, probably like a crocodile, which Yahweh will catch with hooks and throw out to die in the open country. Pharaoh’s claim that he made the Nile, or made himself, was a claim to be a god. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/names/egypt]])

### Trusting in Egypt

The kings of Judah had relied on Egypt for help against Babylon, but Egypt failed them, like a walking stick made of [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/other/reed]] that breaks and wounds the one who leans on it. After its judgment, Egypt would never again tempt Israel to [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/trust]] in it instead of Yahweh.

### Wages for Nebuchadnezzar

[[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/names/nebuchadnezzar]] besieged [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/names/tyre]] for many years but gained little plunder from it. Yahweh says that he will give Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar as payment, because the Babylonian army had been carrying out Yahweh’s judgment.

# Ezekiel 30 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues Ezekiel’s prophecies against Egypt. It contains two messages from Yahweh: a long announcement of the day of judgment on Egypt (1–19) and a separate, dated message about Pharaoh’s broken arms (20–26).

1. The day of Yahweh will bring the sword on Egypt and her allies (1–9)
2. Yahweh will use Nebuchadnezzar to destroy Egypt (10–12)
3. Yahweh will judge Egypt’s idols and cities (13–19)
4. Yahweh breaks Pharaoh’s arms and strengthens the king of Babylon (20–26)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The day of Yahweh

In [verses 2–3](../30/02.md), the “day” that is near is the time when Yahweh comes to judge his enemies, here Egypt and the nations allied with her.

### “They will know that I am Yahweh”

This refrain ([verses 8](../30/08.md), [19](../30/19.md), [25](../30/25.md), and [26](../30/26.md)) states the purpose of the judgment: Egypt will recognize that Yahweh is the true God. Translate it the same way each time.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Nested quotations

The first message ([verses 2–19](../30/02.md)) contains several levels of quotation: Yahweh tells Ezekiel to say what Yahweh says, which includes a command to wail. Consider whether your readers can follow these levels or whether some should be made indirect.

### Names of Egyptian cities

[Verses 13–18](../30/13.md) name many cities in Egypt to show that the judgment will reach the whole land. Spell these names in a way that fits your language and keep them consistent with how you translated them elsewhere.

### Pharaoh’s broken arms

In [verses 21–25](../30/21.md), breaking Pharaoh’s arms represents destroying his military power, and strengthening the arms of the king of Babylon represents making his army strong. Keep this image consistent across the section if your readers will understand it.

# Ezekiel 31 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is a dated message from Yahweh to Pharaoh. It uses the fall of Assyria, pictured as a great cedar tree, as a warning that Egypt will fall in the same way.

1. Yahweh tells Ezekiel to ask Pharaoh whom he is like in his greatness (1–2)
2. Assyria was a magnificent cedar that no other tree could equal (3–9)
3. Yahweh had the cedar cut down because of its pride (10–14)
4. The cedar went down to Sheol, and the nations mourned (15–17)
5. Pharaoh will be brought down like the cedar (18)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### A great tree as a picture of a kingdom

People in the ancient Near East sometimes pictured a powerful kingdom as a huge tree. In this chapter, the birds and animals that live in the cedar and the nations in its shade represent the peoples that Assyria ruled and protected, and the other trees represent other nations and their rulers.

### Sheol and the pit

The “lower land,” “Sheol,” and “the pit” all refer to the place of the dead. The Israelites thought of it as being below the ground, so the dead “go down” to it.

### The uncircumcised

Being buried among “the uncircumcised” ([verse 18](../31/18.md)) was considered a shameful fate, because the Israelites regarded uncircumcised people as unclean and outside of God’s covenant.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Extended metaphor

The whole chapter describes Assyria and Pharaoh as trees. Since Yahweh explains in [verse 18](../31/18.md) that the picture is about what will happen to Pharaoh and his people, it would be best to keep the tree imagery throughout if your readers will understand it, rather than explaining it verse by verse.

### Who is being addressed

Yahweh speaks to Pharaoh as “you” in [verses 2](../31/02.md) and [18](../31/18.md), but describes Assyria as “it” in between. Make sure your readers can tell that the story about Assyria is told to Pharaoh as a warning about what will happen to him.

# Ezekiel 32 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter contains the last two of Ezekiel’s prophecies against Egypt. Each begins with a date, and both are funeral songs over Pharaoh and his people.

1. A lament over Pharaoh, king of Egypt (1–16)
    1. Yahweh will catch Pharaoh like a sea monster and leave his body for scavengers (1–6)
    2. Yahweh will darken the sky, and the nations will tremble at Egypt’s fall (7–10)
    3. The king of Babylon will destroy Egypt’s people and animals (11–16)
2. Egypt goes down to the realm of the dead (17–32)
    1. Ezekiel is to wail over Egypt and send it down to the pit (17–21)
    2. Assyria, Elam, Meshech, and Tubal already lie there (22–27)
    3. Pharaoh will lie among the uncircumcised (28)
    4. Edom, the princes of the north, and the Sidonians also lie there (29–30)
    5. Pharaoh will see them and be comforted (31–32)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Lamentation

A [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/lament]] was a funeral song sung over the dead. Here Ezekiel sings it over Pharaoh before he dies, which shows that his destruction is certain.

### Sheol and the pit

In [32:17–32](../32/17.md), the “pit,” “the lower land,” and [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/hades]] refer to the place of the dead. Ezekiel describes it as a place where defeated nations lie together in their graves.

### The uncircumcised

The Israelites considered it shameful to be buried among people who were not circumcised ([[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/circumcise]]) or among those killed in battle. Egypt practiced circumcision, so being laid among “the uncircumcised” would have been a great disgrace for Pharaoh.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Quotations within quotations

Yahweh tells Ezekiel what to say, and that message contains further words from Yahweh and from the dead in Sheol. Consider how your language can show these levels of speech clearly.

### Nations and their rulers

In [32:22–30](../32/22.md), each nation is referred to as both “her” and “him,” since the text speaks of both the nation and its king. You may need to use one pronoun consistently so readers do not become confused.
