# Ezekiel 33 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter begins a new part of the book. Yahweh renews Ezekiel’s role as a watchman, news arrives that Jerusalem has fallen, and Yahweh then gives messages about the people left in the land and about the exiles.

1. Ezekiel is a watchman for Israel (1–9)
    1. The duty of a watchman (1–6)
    2. Yahweh appoints Ezekiel as a watchman (7–9)
2. Yahweh answers the people’s complaints about his justice (10–20)
    1. Yahweh wants the wicked to turn back and live (10–11)
    2. Yahweh judges people by how they are living now (12–16)
    3. Yahweh’s way is fair, but the people’s way is not (17–20)
3. A fugitive reports that Jerusalem has fallen, and Ezekiel can speak again (21–22)
4. Yahweh condemns the people living in the ruins of Israel (23–29)
5. The exiles listen to Ezekiel but do not obey him (30–33)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The watchman

In ancient Israel, a watchman stood on a city wall or tower and blew a shofar (a ram’s horn) to warn the people when an enemy army approached. Yahweh uses this image to show that Ezekiel must warn the people and that each person who hears the warning is responsible to respond to it. Yahweh first gave Ezekiel this role in [3:16–21](../03/16.md).

### Turning back from wickedness

Verses 10–20 repeat the teaching of [chapter 18](../18/01.md). Yahweh judges each person according to whether he is now doing what is [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/righteous]] or what is [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/evil]], and he wants wicked people to [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/repent]] and live.

### The fall of Jerusalem

The fugitive’s report in verse 21 fulfills what Yahweh told Ezekiel in [24:26–27](../24/26.md). Yahweh had kept Ezekiel from speaking freely since [3:26](../03/26.md), but now he opens Ezekiel’s mouth.

### The claim to the land

The people left in Judah reasoned that since God gave the land to [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/names/abraham]] when he was only one man, he would certainly let them keep it because they were many. Yahweh rejects this claim because they were practicing idolatry, violence, and adultery.

# Ezekiel 34 General Notes

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### God protects the people

God is against those who exploit others. He will protect and take care of his people. (See: [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/peopleofgod]])

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Metaphor

The people of Israel are compared to sheep and God and the son of David as good shepherds. This is a common metaphor in scripture. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-metaphor]])

Yahweh is following the custom of the culture by swearing an oath to indicate the seriousness of what he is saying. According to the custom, people would guarantee the oath by something that they hold sacred, and the most sacred thing would be the life of Yahweh. To do the same, Yahweh is swearing by his own life. Also according to custom, he is stating the first part of a condition (“if”) but not the second part (“then”), which would be the penalty for not telling the truth. Normally the penalty would be understood to be something general such as “may Yahweh punish me severely,” yielding something like, “If it is not because of my flock becoming prey…may Yahweh punish me severely.” But since Yahweh is speaking, stating this would not make sense. Yahweh is following the custom of the culture by swearing an oath to indicate the seriousness of what he is saying. According to the custom, people would guarantee the oath by something that they hold sacred, and the most sacred thing would be the life of Yahweh. To do the same, Yahweh is swearing by his own life in the first part of this verse. After stating what he will do, He then follows the custom to state the first part of a condition (“if”) but not the second part (“then”), which would be the penalty for not telling the truth. Normally the penalty would be understood to be something general such as “may Yahweh punish me severely,” yielding something like, “If you did not hate blood, may Yahweh punish me severely…” But since Yahweh is speaking, stating this would not make sense. It may be clearest to translate the oath as a positive statement. Alternate translation: [I swear that it is because you hated blood]

# Ezekiel 40 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, Ezekiel begins his description of his vision of the restored temple which continues through chapter 48. He describes the outer wall, its gates, the outer courtyard, the inner gates, the inner courtyard, rooms in the courtyards, the altar, and the entryway to the temple building.

1. Yahweh brings Ezekiel to see the temple vision (1–4)
2. The man measures the outer wall and eastern gate (5–16)
3. The man measures the outer court and northern gate (17–27)
4. The man measures the inner court and southern gate (28–49)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The temple complex

In this chapter, God takes Ezekiel in a vision to see a restored temple in the land of Israel. As Ezekiel describes this restored temple, he assumes that his readers already know what temple complexes in his culture were generally like. He simply starts describing what he sees, starting from the outer wall and moving in. The temple complex he describes has an outer and an inner wall. There is an outer courtyard between the two walls and an inner courtyard within the inner wall. Each of these walls has three gatehouses in it, one each on the north, east, and south sides. The gatehouses in the outer wall protrude into the outer courtyard. The gatehouses in the inner wall also protrude into the outer courtyard. See below for a description of each gatehouse. There were rooms around the outer wall and a pavement in front of them. There were some rooms near the gatehouses through the inner wall. Within the inner courtyard, there was an altar and the temple building itself. The temple building was on the far west side of the temple complex, which is why there were no gates on this side.

### The gatehouses

Each gatehouse had the same structures and measurements. There were steps leading to the gateway itself. Behind the gateway, there was a hallway that passed through the rest of the structure. On each side of the hallway were three alcoves with low walls in front of them. For the outer gatehouses, the hallway ended in a porch, which opened onto the outer court. For the inner gatehouses, the porch was in front of the hallway so it too could open onto the outer court. Ezekiel learns the measurements and some of the decorations for all these parts of the gatehouse.

### Ezekiel’s guide

In this chapter, Ezekiel’s guide is called “a man” or “he.” Most scholars think that he is an angel. There are many other stories in this culture about angels who guide a human and show special things to that human. However, Ezekiel does not specify anything about this “man” except that he is bright and shining. Consider how you might refer to this “man” without being too specific.

### Long cubits

In verse 5, Ezekiel states that the man’s measuring stick used long cubits. These cubits were the length of a standard cubit plus one handbreadth. Standard cubits were around 46 centimeters long. A handbreadth was about 8 centimeters. So, these long cubits were around 54 centimeters long. This the length of the cubit that Ezekiel uses throughout the rest of this section. The UST expresses the appropriate measurements in centimeters and meters.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Measurement directions

Ezekiel seems to use the word “width” for the shorter side of a shape and the word “length” for the longer side of a shape. This is particularly clear in [40:49](../40/49.md) and [41:2](../41/02.md). In 40:49, Ezekiel identifies the “length” of the porch as 20 cubits. This measures from the porch from north to south. However, in 41:2, he identifies the “width” of the holy place as 20 cubits. This again measures from north to south. This is not natural in English. Speakers of English usually use the same term for the same compass direction. In this case, an English speaker would probably use “width” for both of these measurements. The ULT follows the Hebrew terms. The UST uses natural English terms. Consider how you might identify directions of measurement in your language.

### Architectural terms and repeated phrases

The exact meaning of some building terms, such as those translated “alcove,” “jamb,” “porch,” and “sill,” is uncertain, and translators may use general terms for parts of a gateway. The chapter also repeats expressions such as “around, around” (all the way around), “from here and from there” (on each side), “whose face was the way of the east” (facing east), and “the way of the east” (east side) which should be translated consistently.

### Corrections of the scribes

In this chapter, later scribes provided many corrections in the margins. Sometimes modern translations follow these corrections, and sometimes they do not. The ULT always follows the traditional consonantal text. The UST sometimes follows the corrections in the margins. In these cases, there are notes that explain the alternative reading.

### Alternative readings

There are several places in this chapter where the traditional Hebrew consonants do not make much sense or do not fit with the other descriptions and measurements in this section. In many of these cases, the ancient Greek translation has a reading that makes more sense. Many translations use the ancient Greek translation in these cases. Translation notes identify these specific cases and provide the alternative readings. The UST often, but not always, follows these alternative readings.

# Ezekiel 41 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, Ezekiel learns about the measurements, decorations, and one piece of furniture for the temple building itself. He also learns about the courtyard around the temple building and a structure to the west of the temple building.

1. The man measures the temple sanctuary and inner room (1–4)
2. The man measures the temple chambers and outer structure (5–11)
3. The man measures the temple building and surrounding areas (12–17)
4. The man describes the temple’s furnishings and decorations (18–26)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Long cubits

In 40:5, Ezekiel states that the man’s measuring stick used long cubits. These cubits were the length of a standard cubit plus one handbreadth. Standard cubits were around 46 centimeters long. A handbreadth was about 8 centimeters. So, these long cubits were around 54 centimeters long. This is the length of the cubit that Ezekiel uses throughout this section. The UST expresses the appropriate measurements in centimeters and meters.

### The temple building

The temple building includes two primary rooms, the “nave” (the Holy Place) and the “holy place” (the Most Holy Place). The Holy Place is a rectangle, and the Most Holy Place behind it to the west is a square. The temple building also has a rectangular entryway. There are side chambers whose back walls butt up against the outside wall of the temple building. The temple building sits on a raised platform or foundation. The whole temple building, including the side chambers, is 100 cubits from east to west and 50 cubits from north to south.

### The “side chambers”

There are three stories of “side chambers.” It is possible that each story was a single, long chamber that went around the outside of the temple building. It is more likely that each story contained 30 individual rooms that went around the outside of the temple building. There is either a ramp or stairs leading to the higher stories. The higher stories are deeper than the lower stories. This may mean that the temple wall narrowed as it went up. It may mean that the upper stories hung over the lower stories. Scholars are not sure what these side rooms were for. They may have been for storing things.

### The “courtyard” around the temple building

There was a small “courtyard” around the temple building. On the north, west, and east sides, there were 20 cubits of space between the edge of the temple building platform and the edges of the courtyard. On the east side of the temple building was the main inner courtyard, which is 100 cubits square according to [40:47](../40/47.md).

### The “structure” to the west

Ezekiel mentions a “structure” on the west side of the temple building, separated by a small courtyard that is 20 cubits wide. This structure has walls that are five cubits thick. Its exterior measurements are 100 cubits from north to south and 80 cubits from east to west. It is uncertain how tall this building was or what its function was. Most likely, its back wall butted up against the outside wall of the temple complex on the west.

### The “altar” or “table”

In 41:22, Ezekiel refers to an “altar,” but his guide then calls it a “table.” Scholars guess that this is the same kind of table that the priests used in the tabernacle and temple to present the special bread to God. In this sense, it is like an altar, since priests use it to present things to God.

### The “doors”

In 41:23–24, Ezekiel describes the “doors” that close the entrances into the Holy Place and Most Holy Place. For each entrance, there are two sets of doors. Most likely, one set was at the front of the sill or threshold and the other set was at the back, leaving a small space in between. Each set of doors had two panels, which were connected to the side walls by hinges. In this way, the panels could open by swinging toward the walls. Consider how you might refer to this style of door in your language.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Measurement directions

Ezekiel seems to use the word “width” for the shorter side of a shape and the word “length” for the longer side of a shape. See the introduction to chapter 40 for more information. This is not natural in English. Speakers of English usually use the same term for the same compass direction. The ULT follows the Hebrew terms. The UST uses natural English terms. Consider how you might identify directions of measurement in your language.

### Unknown terms

In this chapter, there are many technical terms for parts of buildings. Often, scholars can guess what these terms mean. However, sometimes scholars are not very sure. This is especially true in [41:6–8](../41/06.md), [16–17](../41/16.md), [21](../41/21.md). The ULT and the UST provide one of several possible ways to understand these verses. You may wish to follow a major translation in your area.

### Terminology for temple rooms

Throughout this chapter, Ezekiel refers to the two important rooms in the temple building. He consistently uses “nave” for the Holy Place. He uses several words for the Most Holy Place, including “inside,” “inner,” “inner house,” and “holy place.” The ULT follows the Hebrew. The UST refers directly to the Most Holy Place.

# Ezekiel 42 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, Ezekiel learns about rooms that are grouped together into two buildings, one to the northwest of the temple building and one to the southwest of the temple building. He learns that these rooms are for the sacred offerings and clothing. Finally, Ezekiel learns the dimensions of the outer wall of the whole temple complex.

1. The man shows Ezekiel the chambers for the priests (1–14)
2. The man measures the outer boundaries of the temple area (15–20)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The chambers

There are two buildings full of chambers, one to the north and one to the south of the structure and courtyard to the west of the temple building. Scholars agree that these buildings are three stories high, and that the highest story’s rooms are smaller than the rooms in the lower stories. Scholars disagree on many other things about how these buildings were constructed. There is a walkway next to each building, but it is not certain which side of the building it is on. There is a wall near the walkway, but it is not certain exactly where it runs. There are “ledges” on each building, but it is not certain exactly what they look like or what their function is. It is clear that these buildings were for the priests to use while they were interacting with holy places and things. When the meaning of a description is uncertain, consider following a major translation in your area or the reading represented by the UST.

### Holy and common

In this chapter, there is a strong distinction between what is holy, or set apart for God, and what is common, or ordinary. Holy and common places, things, and people are not supposed to mix. Both the wall around the temple complex and the two buildings in this chapter help separate what is holy from what is common.

Instead, a correction written by a scribe or an ancient translation sometimes makes more sense. In these cases, the notes provide the alternative reading provided by the correction or ancient translation. Consider following a major translation in your area or the reading represented by the UST.

# Ezekiel 43 Chapter Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, Ezekiel sees Yahweh return to the temple. Yahweh then speaks to him. He tells Ezekiel about what the Israelites did wrong in the past what he needs to tell them now about this temple. Then, he tells Ezekiel about the altar and the sacrifices required to consecrate it.

1. The glory of Yahweh returns to the temple (1–12)
2. Yahweh gives instructions for the altar (13–17)
3. Yahweh commands the consecration of the altar (18–27)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Yahweh returns

In this chapter, Ezekiel sees Yahweh’s glory arrive at and enter the temple. This is important in the book of Ezekiel because in chapter 10, Yahweh leaves the temple. When Yahweh leaves it is judgment against the Israelites. So, when Yahweh returns, it is repairing the relationship between the Israelites and Yahweh. Ezekiel says that Yahweh’s glory looked like what he had seen previously. These previous visions are in [Ezekiel 1](../01/01.md) and [8](../08/01.md). See those chapters for help in translating terms and ideas in [43:1–5](../43/01.md).

### The altar

In [43:13–17](../43/13.md), the sacrificial altar for the temple is described. Much of this description is difficult for scholars to understand. There are three important decisions that translators need to make. First, is the altar made out of three sections or just two? It is clear that the altar is made up of square sections that are stacked on top of each other. The higher section is two cubits narrower than the section it sits on. What is not clear is whether there are two or three of these sections. The UST models an altar with three sections. Second, how many gutters are there on this altar? It is clear that there is a gutter around the base of the altar. This gutter collects the blood from the animals. This may be the only gutter, or there may be a second gutter at the edge of the highest section of the altar. The UST models an altar with two gutters. Third, [43:17](../43/17.md) indicates that one of the sections is 14 cubits on each side. Which section is this? It may be the highest section or the middle section. The UST models an altar which has a 14-cubit square highest section. The altar also has a square area on the top for burning the sacrifices and horns at the four corner of this square area.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Who speaks in 43:13–17?

In [43:13–17](../43/13.md), there is information about the shape and measurements of the altar. It is unclear who is gives this information. It could be the “man” who has guided Ezekiel previously. It could be Ezekiel himself, writing down what he learned. It could be Yahweh speaking from the temple. Since it is Yahweh who speaks in both the section before and the section after, the UST indicates that Yahweh speaks 43:13–17.

### Pronouns in 43:19–27

In [43:19–27](../43/19.md), Yahweh uses “you” in both singular and plural, “they,” and “he.” The word “you” in the singular refers to Ezekiel, and in the plural it refers to all the Israelites. The pronoun “he” probably refers to any person Ezekiel commissions to do a task. The pronoun “they” probably refers to the priests. The UST models this interpretation. However, some scholars argue that “they,” like “he,” could refer to any person more generally. It is also possible that “you,” while referring to Ezekiel, might mean that Ezekiel needs to have someone else do something instead of doing it himself. Consider following a major translation in your area, or you could follow the interpretation represented by the UST.

As in chapter 1, Ezekiel uses words such as “likeness,” “appearance,” and “like” to describe what he saw because of the difficulty in describing these unearthly creatures. Preserve this indirect way of speaking so that readers know that he is describing a vision of something that is not of this world.

# Ezekiel 44 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the vision of the new temple that began in [chapter 40](../40/01.md). After Yahweh’s glory has returned to the temple, Yahweh gives Ezekiel rules about who may enter the temple and how those who serve there must live.

1. The east gate stays shut, and only the prince may eat there (1–3)
2. The glory of Yahweh fills the temple, and Yahweh tells Ezekiel to pay careful attention (4–5)
3. Yahweh rebukes Israel for letting foreigners serve in his temple (6–9)
4. The Levites who worshiped idols may only do the lower duties of the temple (10–14)
5. The priests descended from Zadok (15–31)
    1. They alone may come near to Yahweh to serve him (15–16)
    2. Their clothing (17–19)
    3. Their hair, drinking, and marriage (20–22)
    4. Their duties to teach and judge the people (23–24)
    5. How they must keep themselves clean when someone dies (25–27)
    6. What they receive instead of land (28–31)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Levites and priests

All [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/priest]]s were [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/names/levite]]s, but not all Levites were priests. Here Yahweh says that the Levites who led Israel to worship idols may guard the gates and slaughter the people’s sacrifices but may not serve at the altar, while only the priests descended from [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/names/zadok]] may come near to Yahweh to serve him.

### Holy and common

Many of the rules in this chapter keep what is [[rc://*/tw/dict/bible/kt/holy]] separate from what is common or unclean, such as the linen clothes the priests must leave in the holy rooms before they go out to the people. Yahweh says the priests must teach the people to tell the difference between these things (see [44:23](../44/23.md)).

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Quotations within quotations

Starting in [44:6](../44/06.md), Yahweh tells Ezekiel what to say to Israel, and that message itself quotes what Yahweh says, so the chapter has several layers of quotation that continue to the end of [44:31](../44/31.md). Translators may want to reduce the number of layers by using indirect quotations. (See: [[rc://*/ta/man/translate/figs-quotesinquotes]])

### Keeping duties

The chapter often uses the expression “keep the keeping” to mean carrying out assigned duties in the temple (see [44:8](../44/08.md), [44:14–16](../44/14.md)). Translators should express this meaning in a natural way and use the same expression each time it occurs.
